text: In 1965, the CIA lost a nuclear device on a mountain in India.
And it was built to spy on China.
A year earlier, China had tested its first atomic bomb, at Lop Nur.
Missile tests would come next, and America wanted to hear them.
But radio travels in straight lines. Mountains block it.
So you listen from as high as you can.
The CIA and Indian intelligence chose Nanda Devi. Nearly eight kilometers up.
The device: an antenna, two radios, and seven capsules of plutonium.
Up there, batteries die. Plutonium doesn't. Its heat becomes electricity.
In October 1965, climbers carried it up. Near the top, a blizzard hit.
They tied it into a crack in the rock, and turned back.
In spring, they returned. It was gone, swept down the mountain.
They searched for years with radiation detectors. Nothing.
In 1978, India's prime minister admitted it in parliament.
As far as anyone knows, the plutonium is still up there, in the ice that feeds the Ganges.
And sixty years later, it's still warm.
